templates.title: Early abandonment by title and country, with a minimum-plays floor
templates.subtopic: gaps and islands with LAG, conditional aggregation, HAVING floors

sections.scenario: A global video streaming service wants to know where viewers give up on a title almost as soon as they press play. A high early-stop rate in one country can point to a missing dub, poor subtitles or artwork that sets the wrong expectation. The player logs every play with how far into the title it got. Small counts are noisy, so a title and country pair is only reported once it has enough plays.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns title_id, country, plays, early_stops, early_stop_rate: one row per title and country with at least {{min_plays}} counted plays, ordered by early_stop_rate descending, then title_id, then country. A play is an early stop when its furthest playback position is below {{n_min}} minutes ({{n_sec}} seconds); a play that reaches exactly {{n_min}} minutes is not an early stop. For a single play, its furthest position is end_position_s. early_stop_rate is early_stops / plays, rounded to 4 decimal places. {{session_rule}} {{resume_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Positions are seconds into the title; stopped_at − started_at is wall-clock time and includes pauses, so it is not how far someone watched. The sample has {{plays}} rows in plays; production has billions of plays a day across every country the service operates in.
sections.assumptions: Titles, profiles, countries, thresholds and the session rule are hypothetical and simpler than any production definition. In this sample all of a profile's plays are in one country. runtime_min is there for context; the query does not need it.
sections.criteria: Playback position, not wall-clock time; strict "below N minutes" and an inclusive floor; the ratio rounded without integer division; deterministic ordering. At Hard: previews removed before sessions are built; sessions by gaps and islands with the gap boundary inclusive; a session judged by its furthest position. At Very Hard: resumed sessions left out of both counts. Can discuss recap skipping, incremental sessionisation across partitions, and causality.

clarifications.q: Can I use stopped_at − started_at as the time watched?
clarifications.a: No. Wall-clock time includes pauses and buffering. Use the playback position, which says how far into the title the viewer got.

clarifications.q: Is the floor inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes. A title and country with exactly the floor of counted plays is reported.

clarifications.q: Is a play that reached exactly N minutes an early stop?
clarifications.a: No. Early means strictly below N minutes.

clarifications.q: Which country does a play belong to?
clarifications.a: plays.country, where it was watched, not where the title was produced.

clarifications.q: Should a title with no plays in a country appear with zeros?
clarifications.a: No. Only pairs with at least the floor of counted plays appear.

clarifications.q: How is the rate rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(early_stops::numeric / plays, 4), half away from zero; avoid integer division.

hints: At the simplest level this is one GROUP BY title_id, country with COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …) and a HAVING for the floor.

To build sessions, compare each play with the previous play of the same profile and title (LAG(stopped_at)), flag the plays that start a new session, and number the sessions with a running SUM of the flags (gaps and islands).
A session's furthest position is MAX(end_position_s); its first play is the earliest by started_at, play_id ((ARRAY_AGG(… ORDER BY …))[1] or ROW_NUMBER).
followups: Product wants the same report for the first 30 seconds and the first 5 minutes, by device type. What changes, and which rows would the floor hide in small countries?
For series, many viewers stop an episode early because they skip a recap or jump to the next episode. How would you separate that from abandonment?
At billions of plays a day, how would you build sessions incrementally when a session can cross the daily partition boundary at midnight?
A title's early-stop rate rises the week its artwork changed. What would you need before calling the artwork the cause?

rules.ask: Your LAG compares a play with the previous one by start time. If two plays of one profile and title overlapped on two devices, is the previous play's stop still the right boundary for the gap?
Someone paused for an hour at minute 1 and then stopped. What does a wall-clock duration say about how far they watched?
What does the floor protect against, and what would you show a product manager for the pairs it hides?
Is the rate the average of per-profile rates or the ratio of the totals? Which one answers the product question, and do they differ here?
What is in the ORDER BY of your ROW_NUMBER, and what happens when two plays of a profile start in the same second?

templates.title: Rising titles: week-over-week share-of-viewing gain per country
templates.subtopic: share of total with window sums, RANK with ties, half-open week ranges

sections.scenario: A global video streaming service wants a "rising this week" signal per country: titles that took a larger share of the country's viewing this week than last week. Share, not raw minutes, because a holiday week lifts every title at once. A minimum number of distinct viewers keeps one household's weekend binge from making a title look like it is rising.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that compares the week starting Monday {{week_start}} with the week starting {{prev_week_start}} (weeks are UTC and half-open: from Monday 00:00:00 up to, not including, the next Monday 00:00:00; a session belongs to the week that contains its started_at). A title's share in a country and week is ROUND(100.0 × its minutes_viewed / all minutes_viewed in that country and week, 2), a percentage; a title with no sessions in the previous week has a previous share of 0. gain_pts is the current share minus the previous share (of the rounded shares). A title is a candidate in a country when it has at least {{min_viewers}} viewers there in the current week and gain_pts > 0. Rank candidates within each country by gain_pts descending with RANK semantics (equal gains share a rank, and the next rank skips), and return every candidate with rank {{top_k}} or better: country, title_id, prev_share_pct, curr_share_pct, gain_pts, gain_rank, ordered by country, gain_rank, title_id. {{viewer_rule}} {{week_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The denominator of a share is every minute viewed in the country that week, including titles that are not candidates. Ties are kept even when that returns more than {{top_k}} rows for a country. The sample has {{sessions}} sessions.
sections.assumptions: Titles, profiles, minutes and thresholds are hypothetical. Share of viewing here is a simplified metric for the exercise, not a published methodology. Countries are the session's country; a profile is one viewer.
sections.criteria: Half-open UTC week ranges; shares over all viewing in the country, rounded as stated; previous share 0 for new titles (no inner join); the threshold on distinct viewers of the current week; gain strictly positive; RANK with ties kept at the cut-off; deterministic ordering. At Very Hard: per-viewer minutes summed across sessions before applying the minimum. Can discuss local weeks, approximate distinct counts near a threshold, launch-day bias and restatements.

clarifications.q: Is a session at Monday 00:00:00 in the old week or the new one?
clarifications.a: The new one. Weeks are half-open: [Monday 00:00:00, next Monday 00:00:00).

clarifications.q: Do titles below the viewer threshold still count in the denominator?
clarifications.a: Yes. The share is of all viewing in the country that week.

clarifications.q: A title had no viewing last week. Is it dropped?
clarifications.a: No. Its previous share is 0, so all of its current share is gain.

clarifications.q: Two titles tie for the last place in the top K. Which one goes?
clarifications.a: Neither. Both share the rank and both are returned.

clarifications.q: Do I rank on the rounded or the unrounded gain?
clarifications.a: On gain_pts, the difference of the two rounded shares.

clarifications.q: Does a profile that watched a title three times count three times toward the threshold?
clarifications.a: No. It is one viewer.

hints: Aggregate minutes per (country, title, week) first; SUM(minutes) OVER (PARTITION BY country, week) then gives the denominator without a second pass.
Put the two weeks side by side with a LEFT JOIN from this week to last week (or conditional aggregation), and COALESCE the missing previous share to 0.
Count viewers from the raw sessions of the current week (COUNT(DISTINCT profile_id), or group by profile first when a viewer needs a minimum), then filter, then rank with RANK().
followups: Viewers in Tokyo and São Paulo do not share a Monday. What changes if each country's week runs in its own local time, and which sessions move between weeks?
At billions of sessions a week, exact distinct viewers per title and country are expensive. Where would an approximate distinct count be acceptable, and where, near the threshold, would it not?
A new season launches on Friday. Is a week-over-week gain fair to it, and what would you compare against instead?
How would you make the weekly result reproducible when late-arriving sessions from offline downloads keep changing last week's numbers?

rules.ask: Two titles tie for first place. With DENSE_RANK, which rank does the next title get, and how many titles end up in the top K?
Two titles have exactly the same gain at the cut-off. Which one does ROW_NUMBER keep, and is that a decision you want the database to make for you?
Which day does date_trunc('week', …) start on in PostgreSQL, and in which engines or settings would that differ?
Which titles disappear when this week is inner-joined to last week, and are they the ones a "rising" list most needs?
At this scale, would you count distinct viewers exactly? What happens to a title sitting exactly on the threshold if the count is approximate?
BETWEEN includes both ends. Which sessions does it put in two weeks at once?

templates.title: Concurrent streams over the plan's limit, per plan and day
templates.subtopic: interval overlap, splitting intervals at day boundaries, self joins

sections.scenario: A streaming service's plans differ in how many screens can stream at the same time (plans.max_streams; the limits here are hypothetical). Playback checks the limit when a stream starts, but races, reconnecting players and clock edge cases mean the check is not perfect. An analytics job measures after the fact how many accounts on each plan actually had more streams playing at once than their plan allows, day by day.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns stream_date, plan_name, accounts_over_limit, peak_streams: one row per UTC day and plan on which at least one account of that plan had more streams playing at the same instant than its plan's max_streams, ordered by stream_date, plan_name. A stream is playing during [started_at, ended_at): at the instant one stream ends and another starts, only the new one is playing. accounts_over_limit counts the accounts of that plan that were over the limit at some instant of that day. peak_streams is the largest number of streams any account of that plan had playing at once during that day. {{day_rule}} {{device_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Over the limit means strictly more than max_streams; exactly the limit is allowed. Each account keeps one plan for the whole sample. The sample has {{streams}} streams from {{first_day}} to {{last_day}}; production has hundreds of millions of streams a day.
sections.assumptions: Plans, limits, accounts and devices are hypothetical. Times are already on one clock (UTC); clock skew between devices is out of scope here. A stream's interval is never empty.
sections.criteria: Half-open intervals and a strict comparison with the plan's limit; concurrency evaluated at the right instants (stream starts, and day starts for streams already playing); per (account, day) peaks aggregated to (day, plan); deterministic ordering. At Hard: streams split at midnight and counted on every day they cover, with a stream ending at exactly 00:00:00 not reaching the next day. At Very Hard: concurrency counted in distinct devices, and open streams running until the snapshot. Can discuss sweep versus self join, real-time enforcement and device clock skew.

clarifications.q: One stream ends at 10:00:00 and another starts at 10:00:00. Were two playing at once?
clarifications.a: No. Intervals are half-open, so at 10:00:00 only the new one is playing.

clarifications.q: Is an account with exactly its limit playing over the limit?
clarifications.a: No. Over means strictly more than max_streams.

clarifications.q: Should a day with no account over the limit appear with zero?
clarifications.a: No. Only (day, plan) pairs with at least one account over the limit appear.

clarifications.q: Is peak_streams only for the accounts that were over?
clarifications.a: It is the highest concurrency of any account of the plan that day. On every row returned, that is an account over the limit.

clarifications.q: Which day does an instant belong to?
clarifications.a: The UTC date of that instant: days run from 00:00:00 up to, not including, the next 00:00:00.

hints: The number of streams playing only goes up when a stream starts, so an account's peak in a day is reached at the start of one of its streams, or at 00:00:00 for streams already playing when the day began.
Cut every stream into one piece per UTC day it covers (generate_series over days), clipped to that day; then every question is per (account, day).

For each piece's start, count the account's pieces that day that cover it (a self join on b.start <= a.start AND a.start < b.end), or run a cumulative sum over +1/−1 events with ends ordered before starts at the same instant.
followups: The self join is quadratic per account and day. When does that matter, and what would you write instead for an account with thousands of streams a day?

The playback service wants to block the extra stream in real time rather than measure it afterwards. What state does it need per account, and how do you keep it correct when a device disappears without sending a stop event?
Devices report times on their own clocks, and some are minutes off. How would that change the measurement, and what would you trust instead?
Product asks how often accounts on each plan would have exceeded a lower limit. How do you answer that from the same data, and what does it not tell you?

rules.ask: For an account with 300 streams in a day, how many row pairs does your join compare, and what would a sweep over start and end events cost instead?
Your comparison includes the end instant. What happens when one stream ends at exactly the second another starts?
A stream starts at 23:30 and runs past midnight with others that started before midnight. Which day does your query say the account was over the limit?
At the same instant one stream ends and another starts. In which order do your +1 and −1 events have to be summed, and how did you make sure?
A player reconnects and the old row stays open for a few seconds. How many streams does COUNT(*) see on that device, and is that what the plan limit is about?

templates.title: Home-page rows without repeated titles
templates.subtopic: hash sets and counters, two orderings, all-or-nothing commits

sections.scenario: A streaming service's home page is a stack of rows ("Trending now", "Because you watched…", "New releases"), each backed by its own ranked list of candidate titles. Seeing the same title in three rows wastes the page, so a page assembler fills the rows greedily: the most important row picks first, and later rows skip what is already shown. A row that ends up nearly empty is not shown at all.
sections.problem: Implement fill_rows(rows, cap, min_fill, genres=None, row_genre_cap=None, page_genre_cap=None). rows is a list of (row_id, priority, candidates) in display order (top of the page first); candidates is a list of title ids in rank order and may repeat a title. Fill the rows in order of priority descending, ties by row_id ascending. A row takes its candidates in order, skipping a title that is already in this row or in a row kept earlier, until it holds cap titles or runs out of candidates. If it ends with fewer than min_fill titles it is dropped: its titles are not on the page and stay available to rows filled after it. {{genre_rule}} {{page_rule}} Return a list of (row_id, titles) for the kept rows, in display order; an empty list if no row is kept.
sections.constraints: Up to 3 000 rows of 150 candidates each in the timing check, from a catalogue of 200 000 titles; 1 ≤ min_fill ≤ cap. Expected: time proportional to the total number of candidates (plus sorting the rows). Checking "already on the page" by scanning lists is far too slow.
sections.assumptions: Row names, priorities, title ids and genres are hypothetical. Real home pages are personalised by models; this exercise is only the deduplicating assembly step, with its rules stated here.
sections.criteria: Fill order by priority with the row_id tie-break, output in display order; duplicates within a row and across kept rows skipped; dropped rows release their titles; cap and min_fill boundaries exact; O(1) membership with sets. At Hard: per-row genre counts with skipped titles still available. At Very Hard: page-wide genre counts committed only for kept rows. Can discuss global optimisation, latency budgets and offline tests.

clarifications.q: Is the output in fill order or display order?
clarifications.a: Display order: the order of rows as given. Priority only decides who picks first.

clarifications.q: A row is dropped. Do its titles count as shown?
clarifications.a: No. They go back and later rows may take them.

clarifications.q: Does a title skipped by one row become unavailable?
clarifications.a: No. Only titles in kept rows are unavailable.

clarifications.q: Two rows have the same priority.
clarifications.a: The one with the smaller row_id (string comparison) fills first.

clarifications.q: A row ends with exactly min_fill titles.
clarifications.a: It is kept.

hints: Sort row indices by (-priority, row_id) once; keep a set of titles on the page.
Build each row in temporary structures and commit them (to the page set and any counters) only if the row is kept. That makes "dropped rows release their titles" free.
For genre limits, keep a counter per genre for the row being filled and, at the hardest level, one for the page; both are O(1) per candidate.
followups: Greedy by row priority can leave a lower row empty that a different assignment would have filled. How would you formulate a page-level optimum, and is it worth its cost per page view?
The page is assembled per profile at request time with a 50 ms budget, and each row's candidates come from a different service. What would you precompute, and what do you do when one service is slow?
Rows are also scrolled sideways: only the first 6 titles of a row are visible without scrolling. Should the deduplication care about that, and how would you change the rule?
How would you test this assembler offline so that a ranking change cannot silently empty the third row for a large share of profiles?

rules.ask: How long does "is this title already on the page" take with your structure when 2 000 rows are already filled?
When does a title enter your set: when the row takes it, or when the row is known to be kept? What happens to a dropped row's titles?
Greedy is what the product rule says. When would you argue for an assignment formulation instead, and what would it cost per page view?
What is your sort key, and how do two rows with the same priority come out?
The rule is greedy and never revisits a row. What would backtracking add here, and what would it cost?

templates.title: Subtitle cue repair after a frame-rate change
templates.subtopic: integer rescaling with exact rounding, interval merging, gap closing

sections.scenario: A streaming service receives subtitle files from many localisation vendors. One delivery was {{rate_story}}, so every cue drifts further out of sync as the programme plays. A repair step rescales the times, applies the offset the vendor reported, and then cleans up the result: cues that now overlap are merged into one, and gaps too short to see as a blank are closed.
sections.problem: Implement repair_cues(cues, num, den, offset_ms, min_gap_ms, dedupe=False). cues is a list of (start_ms, end_ms, text) with start_ms < end_ms. In order: (1) replace every start and end time t by t × num / den rounded half up to a whole millisecond, then add offset_ms. {{offset_rule}} (2) Sort the cues by new start. (3) Merge overlapping cues: walking in that order, a cue whose start is strictly before the end of the current merged cue joins it (the merged end is the larger end, and its text gains the cue's text as a new line, separated by "\n"); a cue that starts exactly at the current end does not join. {{dedupe_rule}} (4) Between consecutive merged cues, a gap greater than 0 and shorter than min_gap_ms is closed by moving the earlier cue's end to the later cue's start; a gap of exactly min_gap_ms stays. Return the merged cues as (start_ms, end_ms, text) tuples, sorted by start. This delivery's rate change is num / den = {{num}} / {{den}}, and min_gap_ms is {{min_gap_ms}}.
sections.constraints: Up to 100 000 cues in the timing check, in a single feature-length file. Expected: O(n log n). Use integer arithmetic for the rescale; merging by repeatedly searching for any overlapping pair is far too slow.
sections.assumptions: Cue text, times, offsets and thresholds are hypothetical. Real subtitle formats carry styling and positions, and real style guides set their own minimum gaps and durations; this exercise keeps only times and plain text.
sections.criteria: Exact integer rescaling with half-up rounding; offset applied before sorting; strict overlap (touching cues stay separate) with the merged end as the maximum; lines in start order; gap closing with the exact boundary; O(n log n). At Hard: negative offsets drop or clamp cues correctly, unsorted input with equal starts kept stable, chains merged. At Very Hard: repeated lines within a merged cue dropped. Can discuss shot-change rules, reading speed, automatic drift detection and regression tests.

clarifications.q: How exactly is a time rounded?
clarifications.a: Half up: (2 × t × num + den) // (2 × den) in integers. Python's round() rounds halves to even, and floats can land a hair below .5.

clarifications.q: Are the offset and rounding applied before or after sorting?
clarifications.a: Before. Sort, merge and close gaps on the new times.

clarifications.q: Does closing a gap ever merge two cues?
clarifications.a: No. The earlier cue ends exactly where the next starts; touching cues stay separate.

clarifications.q: Can a merged cue end before one of its members?
clarifications.a: No. Its end is the largest end of everything merged into it, which is not necessarily the last cue's end.

clarifications.q: What should an empty list return?
clarifications.a: An empty list.

hints: Rescale with integers only. With num = 1001 and den = 1000, a time of 1500 ms becomes 1501.5 and must round to 1502.
Sort once by (new_start, input_position); then a single sweep with "current merged cue" state merges everything, chains included.
Keep each merged cue's lines in a list (and a set, if lines must not repeat) and join them at the end; repeated string concatenation in a long chain is quadratic.
followups: Vendors deliver the same programme in 30 languages, and QC wants every file checked against the picture's shot changes so that no cue starts within two frames of a cut. How would you add that rule, and what data do you need from the video?
Merging two speakers into one cue can exceed the line-length and reading-speed limits a style guide sets. What would you do instead of merging blindly?
The rate change was detected because cues drifted. How would you detect the right num / den and offset automatically from a reference track, such as another language's well-timed file?
How would you test this function so that a change to the rounding rule cannot silently shift every cue by a millisecond?

rules.ask: What does Python's round(2.5) return, and what does 1501.5 become with your code? Show the exact arithmetic.
Two cues have the same new start. Which comes first in your sort, and does that change the merged text?
How many comparisons does that take for 100 000 cues, and what does sorting first let you avoid?
A chain of 500 overlapping cues builds one text by repeated concatenation. What does that cost, and what would you do instead?
A cue starts before 0 and ends after it. What does the viewer see, and what should a cue that ends at exactly 0 do?

templates.title: Byte hit ratio of an LRU edge cache for video segments
templates.subtopic: LRU by bytes, admission policy, versioned objects

sections.scenario: Video streaming services place caches close to viewers, for example inside internet providers' networks, so that popular titles are served from nearby rather than across the internet. A cache serves video in segments: a few seconds of one title at one quality, a few hundred kilobytes to a few megabytes each. Before changing the size of a cache or its policy, the team replays a day's request trace through a simulator and compares the byte hit ratio, the share of requested bytes served from the cache. Request hit ratio matters too, but bytes are what leave the upstream network. You are writing that simulator.
sections.problem:
Implement edge_cache(requests, capacity, admit_on_second=False). requests is a list of (object_id, version, size) in arrival order, where size is in bytes, and capacity is the number of bytes the cache can hold. The cache is least recently used (LRU) by bytes:

  1. A request is a hit if the cache holds object_id at the same version. The segment becomes the most recently used.
  2. Otherwise it is a miss. A missed segment that is larger than capacity is never stored, and it evicts nothing. Any other missed segment is admitted: evict the least recently used segments, one at a time, until the new one fits (used + size <= capacity), then store it as the most recently used.
  3. Return (hits, hit_bytes, total_bytes): the number of hits, the bytes served by hits, and the bytes of every request. The byte hit ratio is hit_bytes / total_bytes. An empty trace returns (0, 0, 0).

{{admission_rule}} {{version_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 300 000 requests and tens of thousands of distinct segments, about 13 000 of them cached at once. Sizes are positive integers, and one (object_id, version) always has the same size. capacity is a non-negative integer. Something close to O(1) per request is expected. A cache kept as a Python list, or a scan for the oldest segment on every eviction, is too slow.
sections.assumptions: The trace, sizes and capacity are hypothetical. Segments are whole objects: there are no partial or range requests. Every miss is served from upstream, so a miss never fails. The simulator ignores time: only the order of requests matters.
sections.criteria: Correct hits and bytes with the exact boundary (a segment of exactly capacity bytes is stored, one byte more is not, and an oversized miss evicts nothing); recency refreshed on hits; eviction in least-recently-used order until the new segment fits; the admission rule counts every earlier request, cached or not; a stale version removed before admission is decided; O(1) work per request with an ordered dictionary or linked list; integer results; sensible answers on multi-capacity simulation, admission trade-offs and policy comparison.

clarifications.q: Does a hit refresh a segment's position?
clarifications.a: Yes. A hit makes it the most recently used, exactly like storing it.

clarifications.q: Can a segment that fits exactly fill the whole cache?
clarifications.a: Yes. A segment of exactly capacity bytes is admitted and evicts everything else. One byte more and it is never stored.

clarifications.q: Does a missed segment that is too large evict anything?
clarifications.a: No. It is served from upstream and the cache is unchanged.

clarifications.q: Do I return the ratio itself?
clarifications.a: No. Return the three integers, so the answer is exact. The ratio is hit_bytes / total_bytes.

clarifications.q: Is the hit counted with the size in the request or the size in the cache?
clarifications.a: They are always the same, because one (object_id, version) has one size.

hints: You need two things in O(1): look up a segment by id, and find the least recently used one. An ordered dictionary or a dictionary plus a doubly linked list does both.
Keep a running total of the bytes stored. Eviction is a loop that pops from the old end until the new segment fits.
For admission, remember every object_id you have seen, cached or not. For versions, decide what happens to the old copy before you decide whether to admit the new one.
followups: The team asks for the byte hit ratio at 20 different capacities. Do you need 20 simulations? What does the stack distance of a request tell you, and why do variable sizes make it harder?
Second-request admission raised the byte hit ratio on the trace. Explain why, and describe a trace on which it lowers the ratio.
Popularity follows a daily cycle and new releases spike at midnight. What would you change in LRU, and how would you compare policies fairly on the same trace?
The real cache has 100 TB and a request rate in the hundreds of thousands per second. What changes when the cache is split across disks and servers, and how would the simulator model it?

rules.ask: With 13 000 segments cached, what does each of those calls cost, and how many times does your loop make it over 300 000 requests?
How do you find the segment to evict? If that is a scan over the cache, what does a burst of misses cost?
Which operation on your structure is O(1) only on average, and does any eviction loop risk running long?
Why return integers here instead of the ratio, and where would floating point hurt when you sum ratios over many caches?
A segment that was popular yesterday has a high count today. How does your policy forget, and what does a new release do to it?

templates.title: Pruning a title's bitrate ladder to its convex hull
templates.subtopic: upper convex hull, dominance, greedy simplification

sections.scenario: A streaming service encodes each title many times, at different resolutions and bitrates, and scores every encode with a perceptual quality metric. Per-title encoding, which streaming services have described publicly, chooses the ladder of encodes that players switch between from those measurements. Only encodes on the upper convex hull of quality against bitrate are worth streaming: an encode below the hull gives less quality per bit than a mix of its neighbours. A nightly job prunes every title's candidate encodes to its ladder.
sections.problem:
Implement prune_ladder(encodes, max_rungs=None). encodes is a list of (title_id, encode_id, bitrate_kbps, quality), in any order and mixing titles. quality is an integer score in hundredths (0 to 10 000) or None. For each title:

  1. Ignore encodes whose quality is None. A title with no scored encode does not appear in the result.
  2. Encodes with the same bitrate and the same quality are duplicates: keep the one with the smallest encode_id (string comparison) and drop the others.
  3. The ladder starts at the encode with the lowest bitrate (the highest quality among those) and ends at the encode with the highest quality (the lowest bitrate among those). Its rungs are the corners of the upper convex hull between those two encodes. An encode is a rung if and only if no other encode has a bitrate at or below its bitrate and a quality at or above its quality, and no straight segment between an encode with a lower bitrate and an encode with a higher bitrate passes through it or above it. So an encode exactly on a straight line between its neighbours is not a rung.

Return a dict {title_id: [encode_id, ...]} with each title's rungs in increasing bitrate. {{budget_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 400 000 encodes across 15 000 titles, interleaved; up to a few hundred encodes per title. Bitrates are positive integers. Use integer arithmetic for every geometric test. Something close to O(n log n) overall is expected. Scanning the whole input once per title, or testing every pair of encodes for every encode, is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Bitrates, scores and titles are hypothetical. Quality scores are comparable across the encodes of one title, whatever their resolution. The ladder is chosen on quality and bitrate only; device limits and codec support are out of scope.
sections.criteria: One pass to group by title; scores of None ignored and empty titles left out; duplicates resolved to the smallest id as a string; dominated encodes removed, including same-bitrate and same-quality cases; collinear encodes excluded through an exact integer cross product; the ladder ends at the lowest bitrate with the best score; O(n log n) with a monotone stack; for the budget, the least-area interior rung removed with ties to the lower bitrate and neighbours updated; credible answers on codec transitions and measurement noise.

clarifications.q: Is an encode exactly on the line between two rungs a rung?
clarifications.a: No. Only corners of the hull are rungs, so collinear encodes are dropped.

clarifications.q: Two encodes have the same bitrate but different scores.
clarifications.a: Only the higher score can be a rung. The other one has a bitrate at or below and a quality at or above it, so it is dominated.

clarifications.q: The best score is reached at two bitrates.
clarifications.a: The ladder ends at the lower of the two bitrates. Spending more bits for the same quality is never a rung.

clarifications.q: Why integers?
clarifications.a: Scores are stored in hundredths. Compare slopes by cross-multiplying, so no division or rounding can turn a collinear encode into a rung.

clarifications.q: Can a title have a single encode?
clarifications.a: Yes, and its ladder is that one encode.

hints: Group by title first, in one pass. Then sort each title's encodes by bitrate, with the higher score first at equal bitrates.
Walk the sorted encodes and skip any whose score is not higher than the best so far: it is dominated. The rest rise in both bitrate and score.
Keep a stack of rungs. Before pushing a new encode, pop the top while it lies on or below the line from the rung under it to the new encode. Decide that with the sign of a cross product.
followups: Why is a point below the hull never worth streaming, even when it has a resolution the hull lacks? When could a product team still want it?
Players switch between rungs as bandwidth changes, and switching cost matters. How would you add a minimum bitrate ratio between neighbouring rungs, and is greedy still right?
A new codec arrives and every title is re-encoded over months. How would you run the pruning so that ladders mix codecs safely during the transition?
Quality is measured on a sample of scenes and has noise of about a point. How does noise change which encodes are rungs, and what would you do about it?

rules.ask: Two slopes are 1/3 and 0.333…. Where in your code could rounding make a collinear encode look like a rung, and how would you compare them exactly?
What is your sort key at equal bitrates, and what goes wrong if the lower score comes first?
Why does each encode get pushed and popped at most once, and what is the total cost per title?
When you remove a rung, the areas of its neighbours change. How do you keep the heap from returning an out-of-date area?
How many times does your code read the full list of encodes, and what does that cost at 15 000 titles?

templates.title: Debug the daily Top-10 ranker
templates.subtopic: restated deliveries, filters, units, ordering and ranks

sections.scenario: A streaming service publishes daily lists of its most-watched titles per country and globally. In this exercise a title's views are its hours viewed divided by its runtime in hours, so that a short film and a long series season can be compared. Viewing arrives in daily deliveries per country, and a country's day can be delivered again with corrections. The analysts have raised several complaints about the ranker. A country's list was empty on a day when a different country's numbers were restated. Titles whose trailers autoplay on the home page climb the list. A 90-minute film's views come out too high. Long seasons rank above short films that more people finished. Two titles with identical views were given different ranks. The ranker below is the suspect. {{scope_rule}}
sections.problem:
Fix top10(rows, titles, day, country=None, k=10) so that it meets this specification. rows is a list of dicts {"day", "country", "title", "kind", "seconds", "batch"}. titles maps a title id to {"name", "runtime_min"}.

  1. Scope. Only rows for day count. With a country, only that country's rows count. With country=None, every country's rows count: that is the global list.
  2. Restatements. For each day and country, only the rows of that pair's highest batch count. A later delivery replaces the earlier one entirely, so a title missing from it has no viewing in that country that day. Different countries can be on different batches.
  3. Viewing. Only rows with kind == "play" count. Rows with kind == "preview" are home-page previews and are not viewing.
  4. Views. Hours viewed are the counted seconds divided by 3 600. Views are hours viewed divided by the runtime in hours (runtime_min / 60). A title missing from titles, or whose runtime_min is None, is left out.
  5. Order and rank. Order by views, highest first, then by title id ascending. A title's rank is 1 plus the number of titles with strictly more views, so tied titles share a rank (1, 2, 2, 4). Compare views exactly. Return the first k titles as (rank, title_id, hours, views).
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 200 000 rows and a few thousand titles, processed in linear time plus one sort.
sections.assumptions: Rows, runtimes and deliveries are hypothetical and simplified. Seconds are positive integers and runtimes are at least 60 minutes. Batches are positive integers. This exercise's views rule is a simplification; check the published methodology before reasoning about any real list.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its business symptom; the latest batch chosen per day and country; previews excluded with the right literal; runtime in hours as a real division; ordering by views with the title-id tie-break; competition ranks for ties, with views compared exactly; the fix stays minimal and linear; adds a check per bug.

clarifications.q: Does a restatement replace rows title by title?
clarifications.a: No. The highest batch of a day and country replaces that pair's whole delivery. A title absent from it has no viewing there.

clarifications.q: If one country is restated, does the global list use batch 2 everywhere?
clarifications.a: No. Each country uses its own highest batch for that day.

clarifications.q: Can two titles tie on views?
clarifications.a: Yes, and they share a rank. The next title's rank skips, as in 1, 2, 2, 4.

clarifications.q: What if fewer than k titles have viewing?
clarifications.a: Return all of them.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Make two countries, restate one of them, and ask for the other country's list.
Compare the literal in the preview filter with the data, character by character.
Work out the views of a 90-minute film watched for 3 hours by hand, then run it.
Which number does the sort use, and which number does the specification rank by?
followups: A delivery for yesterday arrives after the list was published. Do you republish, and how do readers see that a number changed?
Views divide by runtime. What runtime does a series season use, and what happens to its views when an episode is added mid-week?
At 190 countries and every day of the year, this runs as a batch job. How would you make it incremental, and what do restatements do to that?
Two titles tie for tenth place in a published list. What should the list show, and who decides?

rules.ask: Two titles have equal views as fractions but you compute them in floating point in two different ways. Can they come out unequal, and how do you compare exactly?
What is the key of your latest-batch lookup, and what happens to the global list when only one country is restated?
The specification says 1, 2, 2, 4. Which window function gives that, and what do the other two give?
Normalising strings hides a typo in this case. What test would have caught the preview filter before it shipped?

templates.title: Ingesting viewing events from devices that go offline
templates.subtopic: device telemetry, offline replay, deduplication, clock skew

sections.scenario: A streaming service's apps run on smart TVs, phones, tablets, game consoles, streaming sticks and web browsers, about {{devices}} active devices in a day. While a title plays, the app sends playback events: start, a heartbeat every few seconds or minutes, pause, seek, quality change, error and stop. At peak the service receives about {{peak_eps}} events per second across {{regions}} regions. On phones and tablets, members watch downloaded titles with no connection, and the app keeps the events in a local buffer for up to {{offline_window}}, then sends them in a burst when it reconnects. Device clocks are often wrong, by minutes or by years. The events feed several consumers: resume points for "continue watching", viewing history, daily popularity counts and playback-quality monitoring.
sections.problem: Design the path from the device to durable, deduplicated viewing data that each consumer can use. Cover the event schema and what identifies one event, the regional ingestion tier and what it acknowledges, the durable buffer and its partition key, deduplication of retried and replayed events, how you assign a trustworthy time to an event whose device clock is wrong, how late and offline events reach each consumer, backpressure when a reconnect storm arrives, and the health metrics you would watch.
sections.constraints: A device retries until it receives an acknowledgement, so the same event can arrive many times. Events from one playback session can arrive out of order, and part of a session can arrive days after the rest. Resume points need seconds, popularity counts need complete days, and quality monitoring needs minutes. Events carry a profile identifier and nothing else personal. No event may be lost once acknowledged.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, windows and rates are hypothetical. Each app can keep a local counter and a session identifier. You may use common building blocks: a partitioned durable log, a stream processor, a key-value store and object storage with a table format.
sections.criteria: Device-assigned event identity with a bounded, justified deduplication window; acknowledgement only after a durable write; a partition key that keeps a session in order without hot partitions; device time and receive time both kept, with an offset estimate and a rule for implausible timestamps; one log, several consumers with their own lateness rules; admission control and backpressure for reconnect storms; privacy by minimal identifiers and deletion handling; health metrics such as duplicate rate, clock-correction rate, lag and late-event volume; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Which timestamp do consumers want?
clarifications.a: When the viewing happened. You also have the server's receive time, which is trustworthy but can be days late.

clarifications.q: How wrong can a device clock be?
clarifications.a: Usually seconds, sometimes hours, and occasionally a reset to a date years ago.

clarifications.q: Does the device know when it was offline?
clarifications.a: It knows its own clock and can keep a monotonic counter since boot. It does not know the true time while offline.

clarifications.q: Are events for one session always sent by the same device?
clarifications.a: Yes. A session belongs to one device and one profile.

clarifications.q: Can a member delete viewing history?
clarifications.a: Yes. A deleted item must stop appearing in history and recommendations, but aggregate counts already published are not changed.

hints: Give every event an identity that the device chooses: device, session and a sequence number. Then deduplication is a lookup, not a guess.
Record both the device time and the server receive time. Estimate each device's clock offset when it is online, and apply it to the events it buffered.
Consumers with different freshness needs should read the same log, each with its own rule for late data, rather than each having its own ingestion path.
followups: Ten million phones reconnect in the same hour after a regional network outage and upload {{offline_window}} of buffered events. Walk through what each stage does.
A device's clock jumps back by two years in the middle of a session. Which events are affected, and how do you place them in time?
Popularity counts for a day are computed and then offline events for that day keep arriving for {{offline_window}}. What do you do with them?
How would you prove, with numbers, that no acknowledged event was lost during a regional failover?
A new app version doubles the heartbeat rate. What does it cost, and how would you stop that from reaching the bill unnoticed?

rules.ask: What is your partition key? What happens to ordering within a session, and to the load on one partition, when one device type replays a backlog?
How long do you remember event identities, and what happens to an event replayed after {{offline_window}}?
Your watermark advances with the wall clock. Where do events that are {{offline_window}} late go, and who still sees them?
How do you estimate a device's clock offset, and what do you do for events recorded before you had an estimate?
A random id per event makes retries deduplicable. What does it not give you that a per-session sequence number does?

incidents: A regional network outage ends and, in one hour, phones upload {{offline_window}} of buffered viewing; the ingestion rate in that region reaches four times its usual peak (the service-wide peak is about {{peak_eps}} events per second).
A firmware bug on one family of smart TVs resets the clock to 1 January 2000 at every boot, so their events claim to be 26 years old.
A mobile release retries without waiting for the acknowledgement timeout, and duplicate rates rise from 0.2% to 30% for one platform.

templates.title: Daily title popularity: hours viewed, views and restatements
templates.subtopic: batch aggregation, late data, restatements, publishable numbers

sections.scenario: A streaming service publishes, every day at {{publish_at}}, the most-watched titles of the previous day for each of {{countries}} countries and globally, with hours viewed and views. In this exercise a title's views are its hours viewed divided by its runtime in hours. About {{titles}} titles have some viewing every day. Viewing data keeps arriving after the day ends: offline downloads sync later, some devices batch their events, and an ingestion fix can re-deliver a day. Most late viewing arrives within {{late_window}}. The list is read by the press, by partners who licensed the titles and by internal teams, so a published number must be explainable, and a change to it must be visible.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline that turns deduplicated viewing events into the daily popularity tables and the published lists. Cover what counts as viewing (and what does not, such as autoplay previews), the grain and keys of each table, runtime as a versioned input (series seasons, episodes added, re-cuts), how restated and late data change past days, what is published at {{publish_at}} and what happens when the number changes later, ties and ranks, how small numbers are handled, reruns and backfills that give the same answer for the same inputs, and the checks that run before anything is published.
sections.constraints: The published list must be ready by {{publish_at}} every day. A published number is never silently changed: a correction must be versioned and explainable. Any past day can be recomputed from stored inputs. Viewing that arrives later than {{late_window}} must still be counted somewhere.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, windows and times are hypothetical. Upstream delivers deduplicated playback sessions with a profile, a title or episode, a country, start and end times and the seconds actually played. The catalogue provides runtimes and the season structure with effective dates. This exercise's views rule is a simplification.
sections.criteria: Viewing defined precisely (title playback only, by event day); immutable, versioned inputs and overwrite-by-partition recomputation; runtime as a versioned, as-of input; separation of computation and publication with versioned, explained corrections; a policy for late viewing tied to {{late_window}}; ranks and ties defined; small-number suppression that cannot be undone by subtraction; pre-publication checks (completeness per country, runtime sanity, day-over-day changes); reruns that give the same answer; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Which day does viewing belong to?
clarifications.a: The day it happened, in UTC for this exercise, not the day it arrived.

clarifications.q: What is the runtime of a season?
clarifications.a: The sum of its episodes' runtimes. Episodes can be added later, so runtime changes over time; you decide which runtime a day uses and say why.

clarifications.q: Are autoplay previews viewing?
clarifications.a: No. Neither are trailers. Only playback of the title itself counts.

clarifications.q: Can a published number change?
clarifications.a: Yes, if late viewing arrives or a delivery is restated, but readers must be able to see which version they are looking at and why it changed.

clarifications.q: Are there privacy rules for small countries?
clarifications.a: Yes. In this exercise, a country-title figure below a minimum audience is not shown on its own.

hints: Aggregate by event day, country and title from immutable, versioned inputs, and rebuild a day's partition rather than appending to it.
Separate the computation from the publication: a day can be recomputed many times, but it is published on a schedule, with a version, and a later version is published only by a rule.
Make runtime an input with effective dates, joined as of the day, so a recomputation of last month uses last month's runtime.
followups: A title's runtime in the catalogue was wrong for a week and is corrected. What do you recompute, what do you republish, and what do partners see?
Viewing for a day keeps arriving for {{late_window}}. Do you publish once, publish provisional numbers, or wait? Defend your choice to the press team.
A title ties for tenth place in one country. What does the list show, and is the rule the same in every country?
The job must finish by {{publish_at}} for {{countries}} countries. Where is the time spent, and what would you make incremental?
An analyst says the global list does not equal the sum of country lists. Explain when that is correct, and when it is a bug.

rules.ask: A day is restated after a re-delivery. How does your table avoid counting that day's viewing twice?
Viewing arrives {{late_window}} late. Which published day does it change, and when does a reader find out?
A season gains an episode on Wednesday. Which runtime do Monday's views use if Monday is recomputed on Friday?
Which ranking function matches a published rule of 1, 2, 2, 4, and what happens at the cut-off for the list?
A small country's number is suppressed but the global total includes it. Can a reader recover it by subtraction?

incidents: An ingestion fix re-delivers two days of viewing for one country after the list for both days was published at {{publish_at}}.
A catalogue change sets the runtime of a popular season to 0 minutes for one day, and the views calculation divides by zero for that title only.
Offline viewing for a holiday weekend keeps arriving for {{late_window}}, and the Monday list understates a family film by 12%.

templates.title: One catalogue, many countries — seasons, localised tracks and availability windows
templates.subtopic: title hierarchy, localised assets, rights windows per country, as-of availability

sections.scenario: A streaming service offers about {{titles}} titles across {{countries}} countries. A title is a film or a series; a series has seasons and a season has episodes. Each title has an original language, localised names, synopses and artwork in up to {{languages}} languages, and each episode (or film) has its own set of audio tracks (original, dubs, audio description) and subtitle tracks (subtitles, closed captions for the deaf and hard of hearing, and forced narrative subtitles that translate on-screen text). What can be played where is governed by licences: a licence grants a set of seasons or a film in a set of countries for a window, a title can leave a country and come back under a new licence, and a few countries receive an edited version with a different runtime. The rights team changes about {{window_changes}} window rows a week, often days or weeks ahead of the date they take effect.
sections.problem: Design the data model for the catalogue and its availability. Cover: the title hierarchy and its keys; localised metadata; playable versions (a cut of a film or episode) and their audio and subtitle tracks; licences and availability windows, and at which level they attach (title, season, episode, version); how a window change is recorded so that you can answer both "what was playable in country C at instant T" and "what did we believe on date D would be playable on date T"; and the analytical facts that answer "titles and hours available per country per day", "share of available hours with a dub or subtitles in language L, per country" and "titles arriving and leaving next month, per country". Write the availability check for one (episode, country, instant) in words or SQL.
sections.constraints: A window is a half-open interval [start, end) in UTC; in this scenario each country's window starts and ends at local midnight of a single catalogue time zone per country, converted when the window is stored. An episode is playable in a country only if a window covers it there and its version for that country has at least one audio track. Past availability must be reconstructable. Track availability is per version, never assumed from the title.
sections.assumptions: Title counts, countries, languages and change rates are hypothetical. Licence terms beyond countries, dates and seasons (fees, exclusivity) are out of scope. A version is identified by its own id and is immutable once published; a corrected encode is a new version.
sections.criteria: Title hierarchy, versions and tracks, and licences/windows modelled separately with clear keys; windows at the right grain (season or episode, country) and half-open in UTC with the local-midnight rule; tracks per version; a bitemporal or append-only history of window changes answering both "what was" and "what we believed"; a correct availability check; facts at stated grains (title × country × day availability, hours by track language) with an incremental build; each incident contained, quantified and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can different seasons of one series be available in different countries?
clarifications.a: Yes. A licence can cover seasons 1–3 in one set of countries and season 4 in another, or season 4 may not be licensed yet.

clarifications.q: Is a dub available for a whole series?
clarifications.a: Not necessarily. Season 1 may be dubbed into a language and season 2 not yet; tracks belong to the episode's version.

clarifications.q: When a window is changed after it was published, do we need the old value?
clarifications.a: Yes. Reports must show what was promised to a country at the time, and audits ask when a change was made.

clarifications.q: Does a country ever get a different cut?
clarifications.a: Yes, for a small number of titles. The cut has its own runtime and its own tracks.

clarifications.q: Are window boundaries inclusive?
clarifications.a: Start inclusive, end exclusive, in UTC after conversion from the country's local midnight.

hints: Separate what a title is (hierarchy, localised metadata) from what can be played (versions and their tracks) and from where and when it may be played (licences and windows).
Store windows at the lowest grain they apply to, or expand them to (episode, country) intervals in a derived table; decide which is the source and which is derived.
Two time axes: the window's validity in the world, and when the row was recorded or superseded.
followups: Write the availability check for one (episode, country, instant), including a season covered by one licence and a later season by another.
A licence ends at local midnight on the last day of a month in a country whose catalogue time zone is UTC−5. What do you store, and what does the daily "titles available" fact for that day show?
With about {{window_changes}} window changes a week, how do you keep a daily (title, country) availability fact for {{countries}} countries current without rebuilding it from scratch?
Product asks: "on 1 March, what did we expect to have in Brazil on 1 April, versus what we actually had?" Which columns answer it?
A subtitle file is replaced after a translation error. How do versions, tracks and history reflect it, and what does an audit see?

rules.ask: A title leaves a country on the 31st and returns under a new licence two months later. How does a single flag answer "was it playable on the 15th of the gap month"?
Season 4 is dubbed into one language and seasons 1–3 are not. Where does your model say so, and what does a viewer in that country see on season 1?
The rights team moved a window's end date twice last month. Which report needs the earlier values, and how do you get them back?
How do you store a window that starts at local midnight in a country, and what does your daily fact use as its day?
How do you answer "share of available hours with a dub in language L per country" from that column, and what happens when one season's dub arrives later?

incidents: A licence renewal for one season was loaded with the end date treated as inclusive. In {{countries}} countries the season stayed playable one day after the licence ended, and the rights team asks for an exact list of affected countries and hours viewed.

A dub was attached at series level by a metadata tool, so the app offered that audio language for every season. Viewers who chose it on seasons without the dub got the original audio, and support tickets spiked in two countries.

A bulk import of about {{window_changes}} window changes overwrote rows in place. Last quarter's "titles available per country per day" changed in the next rebuild and no longer matches the figures already reported.

templates.title: Accounts, profiles, households and devices — who watched, and under which rules
templates.subtopic: identity hierarchy, profile attribution, kids profiles, household rules, deletion

sections.scenario: A streaming service has about {{accounts}} member accounts. An account pays for a plan; it holds up to {{max_profiles}} profiles, each with its own viewing history, recommendations and settings, and a profile can be a kids profile with a maturity ceiling. Viewing happens on devices (TVs, phones, tablets, browsers, games consoles), about {{devices_per_household}} per household, and a person picks a profile on a "who's watching" screen before a play starts. In this exercise an account has one primary household, and in some countries an extra member can be added to an account for a fee and watches under their own login. A profile can be transferred to a new account of its own, taking its history with it, and a member can delete a profile at any time. There are about {{daily_plays}} plays a day.
sections.problem: Design the data model for identity and attribution: accounts, plans held over time, profiles (type, maturity ceiling, language), extra members, households and the signals that place a device in one, devices and their sign-ins, and the play record that ties a view to a profile, device and account. Decide how a play is attributed and whether that attribution may ever change; how a profile transfer and a profile deletion affect history, personalisation data and aggregates; how kids profiles are protected in analytics; and which facts answer "active profiles and accounts per month", "minutes viewed on kids profiles by maturity rating" and "share of plays from devices outside the account's primary household".
sections.constraints: A play's profile is the one selected when it started. Monthly account metrics already published do not change unless a documented restatement says so. Data from kids profiles is used for personalisation of that profile and for aggregate reporting only. When a profile is deleted, its personal viewing history is removed from personalisation within a stated time, while aggregate counts already published stay as published.
sections.assumptions: Account, device and play volumes are hypothetical. Household placement in this exercise uses coarse signals (network and device activity) and produces a household id per device sign-in with a confidence; how those signals are computed is out of scope, and the model never stores precise location. Rules on extra members and households vary by country and change over time; check current public help pages rather than assuming any one rule.
sections.criteria: Account, profile, device, household and extra member as distinct entities with interval history; attribution frozen on the play at play time; transfer handled without restating published metrics; deletion traced through raw data, features, snapshots and aggregates with a stated deadline; kids-profile data restricted to aggregates with thresholds and access control; household signals coarse with retention; facts at stated grains with clear metric definitions; each incident contained, repaired and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is a profile always one person?
clarifications.a: No. A profile is what was selected; analytics must not claim it is a person.

clarifications.q: After a profile transfer, which account do its old plays belong to?
clarifications.a: Your call, stated. Published account metrics must not change; the profile's own history moves with it.

clarifications.q: Can a device belong to several accounts?
clarifications.a: Yes, one sign-in at a time per app, but a TV can be signed out of one account and into another.

clarifications.q: How long can deletion take?
clarifications.a: Choose and state it. Personalisation and raw history must honour it; aggregates may keep anonymous counts.

clarifications.q: What is an active profile?
clarifications.a: Define it; for example, at least one play of at least a minute in the month.

hints: Keep the identity hierarchy as history: profile → account membership and device → account sign-ins are intervals, not current-state columns.
Freeze the attribution on the play (profile, account, device, household at play time) instead of looking it up later through current state.
Treat kids profiles and deletions as data-governance rules with owners, retention and tests, not as filters someone remembers to add.
followups: Draw the keys from a play to profile, account, device and household, and say which of those links are copied onto the play and which are looked up.
A profile with three years of history is transferred to a new account. Show what changes in each table and what last year's "active accounts" report says afterwards.
Define "minutes viewed on kids profiles by maturity rating" so that it can be published without exposing an individual child's viewing.
A member deletes a profile. Walk through raw plays, personalisation features, a training snapshot taken last week and published aggregates.
At {{daily_plays}} plays a day, which attribution columns do you denormalise onto the play fact, and how do you handle a device that was re-assigned to another household mid-month?

rules.ask: A profile moved accounts in June. Which account does your join give its March plays, and what happens to March's published numbers?
Two people share one profile and one person uses two profiles. What does your "user" mean, and which metrics does that change?
The profile's plays fed last week's recommendation training snapshot and last month's published totals. What exactly do you delete, and what do you keep?
Who can query a kids profile's plays at row level, and what stops a join that re-identifies one child's viewing?
What precision do you store for household placement, for how long, and why is that enough?

incidents: A TV app release sent the account's first profile id when the "who's watching" screen timed out. For a week, plays on those devices were attributed to that profile, minutes on kids profiles dropped, and recommendations for the affected profiles drifted.

After profile transfers launched, monthly "active accounts" for earlier months changed on every rebuild because plays were joined to the profile's current account. Finance had already used those numbers.

With about {{devices_per_household}} devices per household, a change in household placement moved a device family to a new household id for some accounts, and the share of plays outside the primary household tripled overnight for those accounts.

templates.title: Localisation deliverables — dubs and subtitles from order to approved, across vendors
templates.subtopic: work orders, versioned deliveries, QC results, source revisions, due dates from launches

sections.scenario: A streaming service launches about {{titles_per_month}} new titles or seasons a month, each localised into up to {{languages}} languages before its launch date in each country. Localisation is ordered from about {{vendors}} external vendors: subtitle files, closed captions, forced narrative subtitles, dubbed audio and audio description, each per episode (or film) and language. Vendors upload deliveries; each delivery goes through automated checks (format, timing against the picture, reading speed) and, for some types, a human review; about {{qc_fail_rate}} of deliveries fail a check and come back as re-deliveries. The picture can still change after localisation starts: an editorial re-cut produces a new source version, and timed deliverables made against the old one may need to be conformed. Launch dates move, sometimes earlier.
sections.problem: Design the data model that tracks localisation from order to approval: source versions of each episode, work orders (episode × language × deliverable type, against a source version, assigned to a vendor), deliveries as immutable versions, QC runs and their findings (severity, type, timecode), approvals, and due dates derived from each country's launch date. Define the status of a deliverable as derived from events, the invariant that an approved deliverable matches the current source version, and the facts that answer "on-time delivery rate by vendor and language", "first-pass QC yield by vendor and deliverable type", "cycle time from order to approval" and "deliverables at risk for launches in the next 14 days".
sections.constraints: Every delivered file is kept, identified by a checksum, and never overwritten. A QC result always names the delivery and the source version it was checked against. A due date changes when the launch date changes, and the history of both is kept. A vendor sees only its own orders and results.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, vendor counts and failure rates are hypothetical. Rates paid to vendors are out of scope. One work order is assigned to one vendor at a time; it can be re-assigned.
sections.criteria: Source versions, work orders, deliveries, QC runs/findings and approvals as separate entities; deliveries immutable and keyed by checksum; approvals tied to a source version; status derived from events; due dates derived from launch dates with history; precise yield, on-time and cycle-time definitions; vendor-level access; facts at stated grains; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is a re-delivery a new work order?
clarifications.a: No. It is a new delivery (version) on the same work order.

clarifications.q: What does first-pass yield mean?
clarifications.a: Define it. For example, the share of work orders whose first delivery passed every check, by the vendor who made it.

clarifications.q: When a re-cut happens, does every deliverable fail?
clarifications.a: Not automatically. Some deliverables only need their timings conformed; the model must say which source version each approval refers to.

clarifications.q: Can the same file be uploaded twice?
clarifications.a: Yes, by mistake or by a retried upload. It has the same checksum.

clarifications.q: Who owns a due date?
clarifications.a: It is derived: the earliest launch date of the countries that need that language, minus a lead time per deliverable type (your choice).

hints: Separate the order (what is needed, against which source version), the deliveries (what arrived), the checks (what was found) and the decisions (approved, rejected). Status is derived from them.
A source version is part of the key of everything timed; an approval for an older source version is not an approval for the current one.
Due dates are a function of launch dates; store the inputs and derive, or store each recalculation as a new row.
followups: Write the status derivation for one work order: ordered, delivered, in QC, failed, re-delivered, approved, needs conform.
Define on-time delivery precisely when the due date moved earlier after the order was placed. Which due date is the vendor judged on?
A re-cut changes the picture of episode 4 after 30 languages were approved. Which rows are created, which approvals stop counting, and how does the at-risk report change?
With {{vendors}} vendors, how do you give each vendor a dashboard of its own orders and QC findings without copying the data?
At about {{titles_per_month}} launches a month, which facts do you keep at delivery grain, which at work-order grain, and for how long?

rules.ask: A delivery failed, was re-delivered and then the picture was re-cut. What does your status column say, and how do you compute first-pass yield from it?
QC flagged a timing error on a file that has since been replaced. How does a reviewer see exactly what was checked?
The launch moved a week earlier. Does the vendor's on-time record use the old or new due date, and how does your model show both?
The same file is uploaded twice and the second upload fails a newer check. Is that one delivery or two, and which result counts for yield?
Which deliverables need a conform after a re-cut and which do not? Where does your model hold that rule?

incidents: An editorial re-cut moved scenes in one episode after subtitles in {{languages}} languages had been approved. QC passed the re-check because it ran against the old source version, and the subtitles went live out of sync in several countries.
A vendor's upload client retried every upload, so each file arrived twice with the same checksum. First-pass yield for that vendor halved on the dashboard and its account manager escalated.
A launch moved two weeks earlier for one country, but due dates had been copied onto work orders at assignment. The at-risk report showed every deliverable on track until three days before launch.

templates.title: Subscription lifecycle — plans, price changes, pauses, partner bundles and payment retries
templates.subtopic: SCD type 2 plan history, effective-dated prices, state machine, partner feeds, involuntary churn

sections.scenario: A streaming service has about {{members}} paying members across many countries and currencies. Members choose among plans that differ in price, video quality, the number of simultaneous streams and whether ads are shown; they can change plan at any time. Prices are set per plan and country and change from time to time: in this exercise members are notified {{notice_days}} days ahead and the new price applies from their first billing date on or after the effective date. In this exercise a member may also pause their membership for a limited time instead of cancelling. About {{partner_share}} of members are billed by a partner (a telecom or TV provider) that bundles the service and sends activation, change and deactivation messages. When a payment fails, the membership goes on hold and payment is retried for up to {{retry_days}} days before it ends.
sections.problem: Design the data model for the subscription lifecycle: plans and their versioned prices per country and currency, the member's subscription and its plan history as a slowly changing dimension (type 2) with effective dates, the state machine (active, on hold, paused, cancelled with access until period end, ended), billing periods and invoices, payment attempts and retries, partner-billed subscriptions and the partner message feed. Define how a plan change mid-period and a price change are dated, and the facts that answer "members and recurring revenue by plan and country as of any date", "net adds by day: gross adds, rejoins, voluntary and involuntary churn", "share of on-hold memberships recovered within {{retry_days}} days" and "price change impact by cohort".
sections.constraints: The plan and price a member had on any past date are reconstructable. Money is stored as integers in minor units per currency, and currencies are never added together without a stated conversion. A partner's messages can arrive late, out of order or more than once, and the partner's own reconciliation file is the record of what it billed. A member counts as churned only once per ended membership.
sections.assumptions: Member counts, shares, notice and retry periods, and the pause feature are hypothetical; check current public help pages for any real plan or pricing rule. Taxes are carried per invoice and out of scope for revenue. Billing dates are per member, not calendar months.
sections.criteria: Price list, plan history (SCD type 2 with effective and recorded dates) and state transitions kept apart; the notice and billing-date rule encoded rather than assumed; on hold and paused as states with clear churn rules; money in minor units per currency; partner messages applied idempotently in effective order and reconciled; precise net-adds identity; as-of facts with partitioning and interval joins; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Does a plan upgrade take effect immediately?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, yes, with the price difference handled at the next billing date; a downgrade takes effect at the next billing date. Model both.

clarifications.q: When does a member on hold count as churned?
clarifications.a: Only when the retry period ends without a successful payment. A member who pays on day 5 of the hold never churned.

clarifications.q: Is a paused member a member?
clarifications.a: Your definition, stated. Most reports show paused separately from active.

clarifications.q: How does a partner tell us about a plan change?
clarifications.a: A message with the partner's subscriber reference, the new plan and an effective time; duplicates and out-of-order messages happen.

clarifications.q: Which price does a member see on the effective date of a price change?
clarifications.a: The old price until their first billing date on or after the effective date, and only if they were notified {{notice_days}} days ahead.

hints: Keep three histories apart: the price list (plan × country, effective-dated), the member's plan (SCD type 2 rows), and the member's state (a state machine with timestamped transitions).
Recurring revenue as of a date is a function of the plan row and the price row in effect for that member on that date, not of the latest invoice.
Partner messages are events with their own ids; apply them idempotently and in effective-time order, then reconcile against the partner's file.
followups: Write the SCD type 2 rows for a member who upgrades on the 10th, pauses on the 20th, resumes a month later and downgrades at the next billing date.
A price change is effective on the 1st. Show which members pay the new price in that month and how "revenue by plan as of the 15th" is computed.
Define gross adds, rejoins, voluntary churn and involuntary churn so that the daily net adds identity holds, including members who recover from hold.
A partner resends a month of messages, some out of order. How do your keys and ordering prevent double activations and wrong end dates?
At {{members}} members, how do you serve "members by plan and country as of any date" quickly without keeping a daily snapshot of every member forever?

rules.ask: Finance asks for revenue by plan on the 15th of last month for a member who changed plan twice since. How does a plan column on the subscription answer it?
A member's payment fails, they go on hold and pay on day 6. In your model, did they churn and rejoin? What does that do to gross adds and churn?
The price change took effect on the 1st but the member's billing date is the 20th. Which price applies on the 10th, and where does your model encode the notice rule?
The partner's deactivation arrives two days after its reactivation for the same subscriber. Which state wins, and how do you know?
A daily snapshot of every member for years is large. What do you keep at full grain, and how do you answer an as-of question for a date between snapshots?

incidents: A price change was applied to every member from its effective date instead of from each member's first billing date after the {{notice_days}}-day notice. Recurring revenue jumped in the report for members still in a period billed at the old price.

A partner covering about {{partner_share}} of members resent a month of activation messages after an outage. Each duplicate opened a new subscription row, gross adds doubled for that partner, and the next day's deactivations ended only one of each pair.
Members recovered from hold on day {{retry_days}} were counted as involuntary churn and then as gross adds the next day, inflating both churn and acquisition for the month.

templates.title: Binge sessions — episodes back to back, autoplay versus chosen, per season
templates.subtopic: gaps and islands, LAG with a gap threshold, distinct counts per session, views versus plays

sections.scenario: A streaming service records every play: the profile, the title (and the episode, for a series), when it started and when it stopped, and whether it started because the viewer chose it or because autoplay started the next episode after the previous one ended.
