The content team wants to see how each season is watched in runs: how many back-to-back runs reach {{min_episodes}} episodes, by how many profiles, and how much of each run comes from autoplay rather than the viewer choosing the next episode. {{view_rule}}
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query against titles, episodes and plays that returns title_name, season_no, binge_sessions, binge_profiles, episodes_in_binges, autoplay_continuations, chosen_continuations: one row per (title, season) that has at least one binge session, ordered by title_name, season_no. Take each profile's views in order of started_at (then play_id). A view continues the session of the view immediately before it when both are episodes of the same title and the same season and it starts no more than {{gap_minutes}} minutes after that previous view ended (started_at − previous ended_at ≤ {{gap_minutes}} minutes); otherwise it starts a new session. A film, or an episode of another title or season, in between therefore ends a session. A binge session is a session of episodes with at least {{min_episodes}} distinct episodes. Per (title, season): binge_sessions counts its binge sessions; binge_profiles counts the distinct profiles that had one; episodes_in_binges sums the distinct episodes of each binge session; autoplay_continuations and chosen_continuations count, over its binge sessions, the views after the first by start_reason. {{end_rule}} {{feed_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The gap threshold is inclusive and exact to the second. The sample has {{plays}} rows in plays from {{profiles}} profiles; production has billions of plays a day across hundreds of millions of profiles. All timestamps are UTC.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, fictional titles, ids and times. plays.title_id is the series for an episode and the film for a film; episode_id is NULL for a film. Two different plays of one profile never overlap in time. Autoplay starts the next episode only after the previous one has stopped.
sections.criteria: Views cleaned before ordering (and, at the hardest level, one row per play_id and the missing end derived from runtime); sessions built over all of a profile's views with LAG and a running sum; the gap measured end to start, inclusive and exact; season and title both part of the continuation rule; distinct episodes for the threshold and the total; continuations exclude each session's first view; deterministic ordering; can explain incremental sessionisation, late plays and a binge-rate denominator.

clarifications.q: Does a gap of exactly {{gap_minutes}} minutes continue the session?
clarifications.a: Yes. No more than {{gap_minutes}} minutes, inclusive; one second more starts a new session.

clarifications.q: Is the gap measured from the previous view's start or its end?
clarifications.a: From the previous view's ended_at to this view's started_at.

clarifications.q: A viewer watches episode 3, then episode 3 again. Is that two episodes?
clarifications.a: One distinct episode and two views. It counts once towards the threshold and in episodes_in_binges; the second view is still a continuation.

clarifications.q: The season 1 finale autoplays season 2 episode 1 within a minute. Same session?
clarifications.a: No. A session never crosses a season. Season 2 episode 1 starts a new session and, as its first view, is not a continuation, whatever its start_reason.

clarifications.q: A few minutes of another series between two episodes — does that end the session?
clarifications.a: Yes, if that play is a view. Back to back means the view immediately before, across everything the profile watched.

hints: Gaps and islands: flag a view that starts a new session using LAG over the profile's views, then a running SUM of the flag numbers the sessions.
Clean the views before the window function (one row per play, its end, false starts removed), so that "the view immediately before" is the right one.
Aggregate per session first (COUNT(DISTINCT episode_id), continuations with FILTER), keep sessions that meet the threshold, then aggregate per title and season.
followups: Sessions cross midnight and daily partitions. How do you compute them incrementally each day without cutting a session that started yesterday?
Plays from offline downloads arrive days later and can land in the middle of an existing session. What happens to this report, and how would you make it stable?
Product wants a binge rate per season: binge sessions per profile that started the season. Write the denominator precisely.
Autoplay continuations are much higher on TVs than on phones. What would you add to the model to tell an autoplayed episode the viewer watched from one that ran in an empty room?

rules.ask: If your window is partitioned by profile, title and season, what happens to a six-minute episode of another series watched between episode 3 and episode 4? Is that still back to back?
Do you measure the gap from the previous view's start or from its end? What does start-to-start do for a 50-minute episode?
A view starts {{gap_minutes}} minutes and one second after the previous one ended. Does your comparison treat that as a break?
Episode 3 was watched twice in a row. How many episodes does that session have in your query, and does it reach the threshold?
What does received_at tell you about a redelivered play, and why must it not decide the order of views?

incidents: After a TV app release, autoplayed episodes were sent with start_reason 'chosen'. This report's autoplay continuations for every season fell by half overnight, and a product team began investigating a drop in autoplay that never happened.

Offline-download plays synchronised days late were inserted into the middle of sessions, but the daily job rebuilt sessions only within the new day's partition. The same season's binge sessions differed between yesterday's report and a full rebuild with a {{gap_minutes}}-minute threshold.

templates.title: "Continue watching" resume points at global scale
templates.subtopic: per-profile resume points, multi-device conflicts, region failover

sections.scenario: A streaming service has about {{profiles}} profiles; one account holds several profiles and plays on TVs, phones, tablets, browsers and game consoles. While a title plays, the player reports its position every {{heartbeat}} seconds and on pause, seek, stop and app close. At peak, {{peak_streams}} streams play at the same time. Each profile's home page has a "Continue watching" row: titles started and not finished, most recent first, each with a progress bar. Pressing play resumes at the saved position on any device, and a member can remove a title from the row. Members can also download titles to a phone and watch them offline. The service runs in {{regions}} cloud regions; any region can serve any member, and when a region fails its traffic moves to the others.
sections.problem: Design the resume-point service and the "Continue watching" row. Cover the write path from players, the store and its keys, how conflicting updates are resolved when two devices on one profile play (or one was offline), what "finished" means for films and for episodes (and how the next episode appears), the read path for the home page and for the play button, the "remove from row" action, replication across regions and failover, and how this data feeds viewing history and recommendations without coupling them to the play button's latency.
sections.constraints: Resume lookup when play is pressed: p99 under 50 ms. A position saved on one device should be visible to another device of the same profile within a few seconds in the same region. A member must never be moved backwards by more than one heartbeat interval because a stale or delayed update won. Offline playback reports its positions when the phone reconnects, possibly days later. Kids profiles' rows never show titles above the profile's maturity setting.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, intervals and latency targets are hypothetical. Each play starts with a request to the service (to obtain the stream), so the server sees the start of every online playback session. Device clocks are usually right but not always.
sections.criteria: Sizes the write rate and coalesces heartbeats without breaking the one-interval loss bound; keys resume points by profile and title with explicit session and sequence ordering and a stated rule for clocks and offline plays; precise finished and next-episode rules; a precomputed or bounded row read path rather than a scan of history; "remove from row" as a hide marker that a later play overrides; multi-region replication with a stated lag budget and a client-side last-known position as a guard; viewing history as a separate append-only stream; a backwards-jump metric measured from clients; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: If two devices on one profile play the same title at once, which position wins?
clarifications.a: You decide and justify it; people do occasionally share a profile.

clarifications.q: When is a title finished?
clarifications.a: When the end credits start, or when 95% has played if no credits marker exists. For a series, the next episode then appears in the row at its beginning.

clarifications.q: Do offline positions count?
clarifications.a: Yes, when they arrive, but they must not overwrite a newer position made on another device.

clarifications.q: Does "remove from row" delete viewing history?
clarifications.a: No. It hides the title from the row only; viewing history stays. If the member plays it again, it comes back.

clarifications.q: After a region failure, how much position loss is acceptable?
clarifications.a: Up to one heartbeat interval. Resuming from an hour ago is not acceptable.

hints: Compute the write rate first: peak streams divided by the heartbeat interval. Then decide what must be written durably at that rate and what can be coalesced.
Order updates for one profile and title by something the playback session controls (a session id and a sequence number, with a server-observed session start), not by arrival time at the server.
Keep the resume point (tiny, per profile, read on every play) separate from viewing history (append-only, large, used by analytics and recommendations).
followups: What is the peak write rate, and what do you persist per heartbeat versus per playback session?
A phone watches episode 3 offline on a flight while the TV at home watches episode 5. The phone reconnects. What does the row show, and why?
A region fails at peak. What does a member who switches device and presses play in another region a minute later get, and what did you replicate to make that so?
How do you build the row itself (ordering, finished titles, next episodes, removed titles) within the latency target for a profile with ten thousand titles in its history?
How would you prove that members are rarely moved backwards? Name the metric and the client data that measures it.

rules.ask: Last by which clock? A phone whose clock is ten minutes fast sends an older position. Does it win?
What are the partition and clustering keys, and how do you read the row for a profile with ten thousand watched titles?
The queue backs up for two minutes. The member switches from phone to TV and presses play. What position do they get?
After a failover the cache and the store disagree about a resume point. Which one does the play button trust, and how does it notice the disagreement?
What is your merge rule for a position, and can it ever produce a position that no device actually reached?

incidents: A TV app release sends a position of 0 in the first heartbeat of every session, before seeking to the saved point. Within an hour, millions of profiles that watched on that device type see their titles restart from the beginning on their other devices.

One of the {{regions}} regions fails at peak. Traffic moves to the others within two minutes, but cross-region replication was six minutes behind, so members who switch device right after the failover resume up to six minutes earlier than where they stopped.
A mobile release syncs a backlog of offline positions all at once: titles finished days ago jump back to the front of "Continue watching" for many profiles, ahead of what they watched last night.

templates.title: Catalogue search with localised titles and per-country availability
templates.subtopic: multilingual indexing, time-windowed availability, near-real-time updates

sections.scenario: A streaming service's catalogue differs by country. A title can be available in one country and not another; availability windows open and close on dates and local times set by licences, often at local midnight. The catalogue holds about {{titles}} titles (films and series), each with localised names in up to {{languages}} languages, its original title, cast and crew, genres, and maturity ratings that differ by country. Members search from TV remotes (letter by letter, so prefixes matter), phones and browsers, usually in their profile's language, sometimes in another script, often misspelled. Search peaks at {{qps}} queries per second worldwide. Catalogue editors, the licensing system and the localisation pipeline change titles, names and windows throughout the day.
sections.problem: Design the search and discovery index. Cover the indexed document (titles, localised names, people, genres, per-country windows, maturity), how changes reach the index within {{freshness}}, how queries match (prefix, typo tolerance, transliteration, several languages), how country availability and profile maturity are enforced, the ranking inputs, what a member sees for a title that is not available in their country, and how the index is rebuilt without downtime.
sections.constraints: A title must stop being returned as playable in a country within one minute of its window ending there, whatever the pipeline lag. Kids profiles must never see a title above their maturity level, including in autocomplete suggestions. Search p99 under 100 ms. Search must keep working if any single region fails.
sections.assumptions: All counts, rates and targets are hypothetical. A personalisation service returns a score per profile for a list of up to a few hundred candidate title ids in under 20 ms. Playback separately checks the licence before streaming.
sections.criteria: A document model with per-country windows stored as instants converted from local time, and maturity per country; query-time filtering on country, window and maturity before top-K; prefix, typo and transliteration matching with per-language analysers and fallbacks to original and English names; two-stage ranking with personalisation on a bounded candidate set; a change stream with a stated freshness, plus query-time enforcement so lag cannot extend a licence; cache keys that include country, language and maturity and expire at the earliest window end; rebuilds by snapshot plus replay with an alias switch; per-region replicas with no single-region dependency; quality metrics per country and script; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Are window boundaries exact to the minute?
clarifications.a: Licences state a date and a local time per country; the business wants removal within a minute of the boundary.

clarifications.q: Should titles unavailable in my country appear at all?
clarifications.a: Never with a play button. A search for one should show related titles that are available. Titles announced as coming soon may appear with a reminder option.

clarifications.q: Do we search people and genres too?
clarifications.a: Yes: actors, directors and genres, each leading to titles available in the member's country.

clarifications.q: Which languages does a member search in?
clarifications.a: Mostly the profile language, but names in the original language and in English are commonly typed too.

hints: Availability is a time window. Store the windows in the index and filter by the current time at query time, rather than relying on an update event arriving exactly at the boundary.
Separate matching (which titles are candidates) from ranking (their order), and apply the hard filters (country, window, maturity) before you truncate to the top K.
Analysers (tokenisation, diacritics, transliteration) are part of the index schema. Changing one means a rebuild, so plan rebuilds as a second index with an alias switch.
followups: Sketch the indexed document for one title. Where do per-country windows and maturity ratings live, and how large does the document get?
A licence ends at 00:00 local time in one country while the indexing pipeline is 20 minutes behind. Walk through what a member there sees at 00:01.
A member on a TV types three letters with the remote. How do you return good suggestions in under 100 ms across {{languages}} languages?
A new transliteration analyser needs a full rebuild while editors keep changing titles. How do you rebuild and switch without losing their updates?
How would you measure search quality per country and language, and catch a regression that affects only one script?

rules.ask: One index for all countries or one per country? What does each cost when one title's windows change in 150 countries at once?
The change stream is 20 minutes behind at a window boundary. Does the title stay searchable past its licence end in your design?
You filter after taking the top K. A kids profile types a common word and the top 50 matches are all mature titles. What does it see?
What is your cache key, and how do you keep a cached result from showing a title whose window has just closed?
How many index copies is that, and how do you apply one title edit to all of them consistently?

incidents: A popular series' window ends at local midnight in one country, but the index stores availability as dates in UTC. For several hours members there still find it in search and press play, and playback fails with a licence error.

The localisation pipeline publishes names in all {{languages}} languages for a new release in one batch; a malformed file sets the name to an empty string in one language, and on launch day the title cannot be found by name in that language.

After a change that moved the maturity check from the index query into a later processing step, a cache in front of autocomplete serves kids profiles suggestions that include a mature title's name for 30 minutes.

templates.title: Media encoding asset catalogue and re-encode campaigns
templates.subtopic: immutable assets, lineage, lifecycle states, campaign tracking

campaign: re-encoding the back catalogue with a newer video codec
re-encoding every HDR title with new encoder settings
re-encoding the lowest bitrates of every title for mobile networks

sections.scenario: Each film or episode arrives as a high-quality source file and is encoded into many renditions: video at several resolutions and bitrates in several codecs, HDR and SDR versions, audio in several codecs and languages, and subtitle files. An asset has about {{renditions}} renditions; the catalogue holds {{assets}} assets and about {{petabytes}} PB of encoded media in object storage. Every video rendition carries quality scores from a perceptual quality metric, computed per shot and for the whole file. Devices receive a manifest listing the renditions they can play. The encoding team runs campaigns, such as {{campaign}}, that create new renditions for many assets over several weeks and retire the old ones.
sections.problem: Design the asset catalogue. Cover the data model for sources, renditions, encoding recipes, quality scores and QC results, with their lineage; the lifecycle of a rendition from requested to deleted; how the set of renditions a manifest may use is chosen and switched; campaign planning and tracking (done, failed, retried, cost, quality gained); safe retirement and deletion of superseded files; and the queries the encoding team and finance need.
sections.constraints: A rendition is never served before it passes QC (automated checks, plus human review for some titles). A re-delivered source (for example with corrected colour) invalidates every rendition made from the previous version. Devices and edge caches may hold a manifest for up to 24 hours, so a file a manifest references must stay downloadable that long. Campaigns must be resumable and must never redo work that already succeeded.
sections.assumptions: All counts, sizes and durations are hypothetical. Media files live in object storage; the catalogue holds metadata, locations, checksums and states, not the media. The quality metric is versioned and is updated from time to time.
sections.criteria: Immutable rendition records identified by full recipe and source version, with checksums and storage locations; QC results and quality scores as separate records keyed by metric version; explicit lifecycle states with publication only from an approved state, enforced where live sets are written; versioned live sets switched atomically per asset and served to manifests through a replicated read path; source re-delivery handled by lineage queries; campaigns as plans plus task ledgers with idempotent, resumable tasks and per-task cost; deletion gated on references, the manifest cache window and a recoverable soft delete; consistency between object store and catalogue; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can a rendition be modified after it is made?
clarifications.a: Treat files as immutable. A change is a new rendition.

clarifications.q: Who reads the catalogue?
clarifications.a: The manifest service (on every play, through caches), the encoding pipeline, QC tools, campaign dashboards, and finance for compute and storage cost by title and campaign.

clarifications.q: Are quality scores comparable across metric versions?
clarifications.a: No. Scores are comparable only within one metric version.

clarifications.q: How are failures in a campaign handled today?
clarifications.a: With spreadsheets and reruns of whole batches. The team wants something better.

hints: Identify a rendition by its full recipe: source version, codec and profile, resolution, bitrate, encoder version and parameters. Re-encoding creates new records; nothing is updated in place.
Separate a rendition's lifecycle state from the asset's live set (the renditions manifests may use), and switch live sets as whole, versioned records.
A campaign is a plan (which assets, which recipes) plus a ledger of task outcomes, so progress, retries and cost become queries.
followups: Name the main entities and their keys. How do you know which source version and encoder version produced a given file?
Halfway through the campaign, sources for 300 episodes are re-delivered with corrected colour. What happens to renditions in flight and to the live ones?
How does the manifest service get the live set at play time without reading the catalogue database on every play?
When is it safe to delete the files superseded by the campaign, and how do you prove that nothing still references them?
Finance asks what the campaign cost and what it bought. Which queries answer that, and against which quality metric version?

rules.ask: You update a rendition's row in place after re-encoding. A device holds yesterday's manifest pointing at it. What does it download?
The upload succeeds but the catalogue write fails, or the reverse. How do the catalogue and the object store stay consistent?
What exact condition allows a file to be deleted, and who can override it?
The quality metric gets a new version halfway through the campaign. How do you compare old and new renditions fairly?
The campaign is 60% done when a bug is found in one codec profile of the encoder. How do you find and redo exactly the affected renditions?

incidents: During the campaign ({{campaign}}), a scheduling bug adds new renditions to live sets before automated QC has finished; on one device family, 2% of plays of the affected titles show corrupted green frames until the renditions are pulled.

A cleanup job deletes superseded renditions 12 hours after each asset's live set switched, while manifests cached for up to 24 hours still reference them; plays started from those manifests fail over to other renditions at lower quality, and some fail outright.

The quality metric is upgraded mid-campaign. The campaign dashboard compares new renditions scored with the new version against old renditions scored with the old one, and reports a quality gain that disappears when both are scored with the same version.

templates.title: Pre-positioning titles on edge caches overnight, and measuring it
templates.subtopic: demand forecasting, capacity-constrained placement, offload metrics

sections.scenario: A streaming service delivers video from its own content delivery network: cache servers installed inside internet providers' networks and at internet exchange points, grouped into {{sites}} sites. Each site holds about {{cache_tb}} TB, while the encoded catalogue is about {{catalogue_pb}} PB, so a site can hold only a small fraction of it. Rather than filling caches only when a member asks for something, the service fills them ahead of time during each site's quiet hours, a fill window of about {{fill_hours}} hours of local night, choosing which renditions of which titles to place where. A play that misses its site is served from a larger upstream site, which uses provider and transit capacity and can lower the quality the member gets.
sections.problem: Design the system that decides each night what every site should hold, and that measures whether it worked. Cover demand prediction per title, rendition and site (including new releases with no history), the placement decision under storage and fill-bandwidth limits, how the decision reaches the caches and how they fetch, what happens during the day when the prediction was wrong, and the metrics, defined precisely, that show whether placement is good.
sections.constraints: Fill traffic must stay inside each site's window and within a bandwidth budget agreed with the provider. A cache must never evict a file it is currently serving. Fill windows are staggered by time zone, and the decision for each site must be ready before its window opens. Some new releases launch at the same moment in every country, which is mid-afternoon in some time zones.
sections.assumptions: All counts, sizes and windows are hypothetical. Request logs from every site (rendition requested, bytes served, hit or miss) arrive within an hour. Each site's audience uses a known mix of devices, so only some codecs and resolutions are requested there.
sections.criteria: Forecasts per title and country distributed to sites by audience and device mix, with priors for new releases and explicit uncertainty; placement per site by value per byte under storage and fill budgets, with stickiness for files already present; prioritised fill lists that degrade gracefully when a window is cut; an intra-day correction path with its own budget; byte-based offload and quality outcomes as the primary metrics, with fill efficiency and forecast error alongside; policy evaluation by offline replay of logs and controlled rollouts with a stated counterfactual; compute that finishes per staggered window; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does a site hold every rendition of a title it holds?
clarifications.a: No. You choose per rendition; a site whose audience is mostly on phones needs different files from one serving mostly TVs.

clarifications.q: Can a cache still fetch on demand during the day?
clarifications.a: Yes, a miss can be filled from an upstream site, but that uses daytime capacity the providers want kept small.

clarifications.q: What do we know about a new release before launch?
clarifications.a: Only pre-launch signals: similar titles' history, trailer views, marketing plans per country. Say how you deal with the uncertainty.

clarifications.q: How often can placement change?
clarifications.a: Once a night per site is the norm; you may propose more, with its cost.

hints: Demand is heavily skewed: a small share of files serves most bytes. Decide on value per byte stored (predicted bytes served from this site divided by file size), not on title popularity alone.
Placement is a capacity-constrained selection per site with two budgets: storage, and the fill bytes available tonight. A file already on the site costs no fill bytes.
Measure in bytes: the share of bytes the site served itself (byte offload). A request hit ratio flatters small files.
followups: What are the inputs to tonight's decision for one site, and how do you turn a forecast into a ranked list of files that fits {{cache_tb}} TB?
A title launches globally tomorrow with no viewing history. Which sites get which of its renditions, and how sure are you?
A site's fill window is cut short by maintenance at the provider. What is filled first, and how was that order decided?
How do you evaluate a new placement algorithm against the current one without risking a bad night across the whole network?
Leadership asks whether pre-positioning is worth its cost compared with filling on demand. What do you measure, and what is the counterfactual?

rules.ask: If caches can manage themselves on demand with LRU, what does overnight placement add, and how would you measure the difference?
A request hit ratio or a byte hit ratio? A site serves many small audio and subtitle files and few large 4K files. Which number misleads, and how?
On its second day a surprise hit gets five times the forecast demand. How quickly does placement correct, and through what path?
With thousands of sites and millions of files, does your solver finish before the first fill window opens? What do you give up for speed?
Two placement policies run on different sites. How do you make the comparison fair when the sites differ in size and audience?

incidents: On its second day a surprise hit draws five times its forecast demand in one region. Many sites there miss on its renditions during the evening peak, and on-demand fills from upstream sites saturate provider links.

Maintenance at a provider cuts one large site's fill window from {{fill_hours}} hours to 2. The night's fill completes about a third of the planned bytes, and the next evening's offload at that site drops sharply.

A dashboard reports a 97% hit ratio for a new placement policy. It counts requests; measured in bytes, offload fell, because the policy favours small audio and subtitle files over large video renditions.

templates.title: Live-event voting and reactions from millions of viewers
templates.subtopic: burst ingestion, exactly-once counting, fairness under stream delay

sections.scenario: A streaming service broadcasts live events, such as a talent show or a live special. At set moments the host opens a vote: viewers choose one of {{options}} options on their TV, phone or browser within a {{window}}-second window, and the result is revealed on air a few minutes later and shown in the app. Viewers can also send emoji reactions, shown back to everyone as a live reaction meter. Peak audience is {{viewers}} concurrent streams, and viewers watch at different delays behind the live broadcast ({{delay}}), depending on device, network and buffering.
sections.problem: Design vote and reaction collection and counting. Cover how the vote window is presented on the client, ingestion, deduplication (one counted vote per eligible profile per poll), counting with a final result that is reproducible and auditable, the path to the on-air reveal, reactions aggregated in near real time, and protection against scripted or duplicated voting. Say what "fair" means in your design and how you would prove the count afterwards.
sections.constraints: The final count must be ready within two minutes of the window closing and be reproducible from stored records. A vote counts only if it was cast while the vote was open in the stream the viewer was watching. Clients retry failed requests. Reactions may be approximate and lossy; votes may not be lost or double counted.
sections.assumptions: All audience sizes, rates and timings are hypothetical. Every request carries a signed token identifying the account, profile and playback session.
sections.criteria: Separate durable vote and lossy reaction paths; a peak-rate estimate that drives the design; idempotent votes keyed by poll and profile with last-choice semantics; a window defined by stream position with a server-side bound, and a stated fairness rule; durable acknowledgement before counting, partitioning that avoids hot options, and a final count gated on every region's watermark; approximate running counts clearly labelled; eligibility and anti-automation tied to authenticated, actively playing sessions; an auditable vote log that allows an independent recount; pre-agreed policies for disruptions; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: One vote per what?
clarifications.a: One vote per profile per poll; profiles on the same account vote separately. Kids profiles are not eligible.

clarifications.q: Can a viewer change their vote?
clarifications.a: Yes, until their window closes; the last choice counts.

clarifications.q: Viewers are behind live by different amounts. When does the window close for each of them?
clarifications.a: That is the core fairness question. Propose a rule and defend it.

clarifications.q: Do producers need counts during the window?
clarifications.a: They want approximate running counts in the control room. The reveal uses only the final count.

clarifications.q: Are reactions ever used for results?
clarifications.a: No. The meter shows approximate rates only.

hints: Votes and reactions need different guarantees, so give them different paths: a durable, idempotent path for votes and an aggregated, sampled path for reactions.
Tie the window to the stream: open and close markers can travel inside the video stream, so each client opens and closes the vote at the same point in what it shows. Add a server-side bound as well.
Key each vote by (poll, profile) with a client sequence number, so retries and changed votes resolve to exactly one final choice.
followups: Estimate the peak vote rate. Where does your design hit its first limit?
A viewer near the maximum delay votes 20 seconds after the vote closed in the live broadcast. Does it count, and how does your server know?
One ingestion region loses its connection to the counting tier during the window. What happens to those votes, and how is the final count still correct?
How do you detect and handle scripted voting from a small number of accounts or devices?
After the show, someone disputes the result. What can you produce to prove it?

rules.ask: How is the vote topic partitioned? What happens to one partition if you key by option and one option takes most of the votes?
A counter node fails mid-window. How do you rebuild the exact count, and can a retried vote be counted twice?
Whose clock decides whether a vote was on time: the device's, the server's, or the stream's? What can each one get wrong?
Your bot defence blocks real viewers in a country where many people share mobile IP addresses. How would you find out, and what is the trade-off?
Which numbers in your design may be approximate and which must be exact? Point to the component where one becomes the other.

incidents: When the vote opens, clients on one TV platform retry every failed submission immediately with no backoff. The ingestion tier sees six times the expected request rate in the first ten seconds and starts rejecting votes from every platform.
One ingestion region loses its link to the counting tier for 20 seconds during the {{window}}-second window; the votes it accepted arrive at the counters after the window has closed everywhere else.

A stream encoder in one region inserts the vote-close marker 25 seconds late, so viewers on that feed can vote 25 seconds longer than everyone else. The leading option's margin is smaller than the number of votes cast in those extra seconds.

templates.title: A mandatory review gate that every team waits on
templates.subtopic: removing a control safely, evidence, replacing what it protected

gate: every schema change to the shared viewing-history tables needs approval from a weekly review board, introduced after a column rename silently broke the daily title-popularity numbers
any new pipeline that reads playback events needs a manual sign-off from the data platform team, introduced after a job copied events with device identifiers into an unprotected bucket
every new experiment metric needs approval from a central analytics group, introduced after a metric defined the wrong way round reversed the conclusion of a large test

sections.scenario: You lead data platform engineering for the streaming service's viewing data. Two years ago a rule was introduced: {{gate}}. Today the median wait for approval is {{wait}}, and {{teams}} teams depend on it. Some teams have started working around the gate by copying data into their own tables, which the gate never sees. Your director has asked you to remove or replace the gate this quarter. The people who run it believe it is the only thing preventing the original incident from happening again.
sections.problem: How do you approach it? Cover how you find out what the gate actually catches today, what replaces each protection it provides, how you roll the change out and how you could roll it back, how you bring along both the reviewers and the teams who wait on them, how you will know whether things got worse, and what you do if an incident happens after the change. Then tell me about a real time you removed or simplified a process or control, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The original incident must not recur. You do not manage the reviewers. The teams' workarounds carry risks of their own. You have two engineers for this for one quarter.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Establishes what the gate catches from evidence (ticket analysis, near misses, the workarounds) before deciding; replaces each protection with an automated check, an after-the-fact audit or a narrow human review, rather than simply deleting it; reversible, measured rollout with stop criteria; treats the reviewers, especially the gate's author, as partners whose knowledge goes into the checks; addresses the existing workarounds; a clear plan for the first incident afterwards that neither panics nor ignores it; real example with measurable outcome and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is there data on what the gate rejects?
clarifications.a: Every review is a ticket with its outcome and comments. Nobody has analysed them.

clarifications.q: Do the reviewers want to keep the gate?
clarifications.a: Most do. One of them built it after the original incident and feels personally responsible for it.

clarifications.q: Who decides?
clarifications.a: Your director, who wants a recommendation backed by evidence.

clarifications.q: Could the gate stay for some changes?
clarifications.a: Yes; that is your call to make and justify.

hints: Treat the gate as a bundle of checks. For each one, ask what it caught in the last year and whether it could be caught automatically, after the fact, or only by a person.
The workarounds are evidence: the risk the gate exists for may already be leaking around it.
Change it in steps you can reverse: a pilot group, measured outcomes, then wider.
followups: What would you look for in two years of review tickets, and what finding would change your plan?
Which protections become automated checks, which become audits after the fact, and which stay as human review for a narrow set of changes?
How do you work with the reviewer who built the gate?
Three weeks after the change, a change that would once have been reviewed breaks a downstream report. What do you do, and do you bring the gate back?
In your real example, how did you measure whether removing the control was the right call?

rules.ask: Which of the gate's past catches would your automated checks miss, and who notices those now?
Which teams go first, why them, and what result would make you stop?
Name one thing the gate caught that nothing in your plan would catch. If there is none, how did you check?
What do you do about the copies teams have already made outside the gate?
What did you personally decide, and who disagreed with it?

templates.title: Inheriting a team whose last two projects were cancelled
templates.subtopic: trust, diagnosis, choosing the next commitment after a reorg

projects: a real-time viewing-metrics pipeline and a replacement for the nightly title-popularity job
a new device-telemetry schema and a self-service query layer for playback quality data
a feature store for recommendation models and a backfill tool for viewing history
signal: two engineers have asked to transfer to other teams
nobody has left, but on-call handovers are missed and code reviews take weeks

sections.scenario: After a reorganisation you now lead a team of {{size}} engineers that runs the data infrastructure behind viewing analytics. In the past year the team's last two projects, {{projects}}, were cancelled after months of work. The team now mostly reacts to pipeline failures and requests. On top of that, {{signal}}. Your director wants a direction from you within 30 days and visible results within {{months}} months.
sections.problem: How do you lead the team from here? Cover your first weeks, how you find out why the projects were cancelled and what part the team played, how you choose what the team commits to next, how you rebuild trust with the team and with its stakeholders, how you handle the people concerns, and how you will know it is working. Then tell me about a real time you took over a team or project in trouble, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: No new hires this half. The existing pipelines must keep running. You did not choose the team, and the team did not choose you.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Listens before deciding and builds an evidence-based account of the cancellations, including the team's own part; protects running pipelines while reducing reactive load; chooses a small, valuable, written commitment agreed with the people who could cancel it, with milestones and an explicit process for priority changes; honest, respectful conversations about the team's contribution; deliberate attention to the at-risk engineers and to on-call health; measures progress beyond self-report (delivery against milestones, stakeholder confidence, on-call load, retention); real example with personal actions and measurable result, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Why were the projects cancelled?
clarifications.a: Accounts differ. The team says priorities changed under them; stakeholders say the projects were late and kept changing scope.

clarifications.q: How strong is the team?
clarifications.a: Mixed: two strong senior engineers, the rest mid-level. Form your own view.

clarifications.q: Do stakeholders still need what the projects promised?
clarifications.a: Some of it. One stakeholder team has built its own workaround.

clarifications.q: Does the director have a view?
clarifications.a: The director thinks the team over-engineers; you have not seen evidence either way yet.

hints: Before deciding anything, listen: each engineer, each main stakeholder, and the written history of both projects.
Separate what the team controlled (estimates, scope, delivery) from what it did not (priority changes) before you assign any lesson.
The next commitment should be small enough to finish, valuable enough to matter, and agreed in writing with the people who could cancel it.
followups: What do you do in your first two weeks, and what are you trying to learn?
You find the team did contribute to both cancellations through scope growth. How do you raise it with them without destroying what morale is left?
How do you choose the first commitment, and how do you protect it from becoming the third cancelled project?
One of the two strongest engineers tells you privately that they are thinking of leaving. What do you do?
In your real example, what did you change in how the team committed to work, and what was the measurable result?

rules.ask: What do you ask in those conversations, and what do you do with an answer that contradicts your director's view?
Which win, how small, and why would anyone outside the team care about it?
Who signs off the priorities, and what do you do the next time they change halfway through?
How would you know morale is improving, apart from people telling you so?
How do you separate an engineer's performance from the effect of two cancelled projects?

templates.title: A senior engineer whose reviews stall everyone else
templates.subtopic: code review culture, feedback, protecting quality and growth

engineer: the person who designed the streaming ingestion of playback events
the team's most experienced person on the title-popularity pipeline
a senior engineer who is the only expert on the encoding-metadata service
signal: changes to the core pipeline wait a median of 9 days for approval
two mid-level engineers have asked to move off the codebase
a new hire's first three changes were rejected with one-line comments
role: the tech lead on the same team, not their manager
a staff engineer on a neighbouring team that depends on the code

sections.scenario: The engineer in question is {{engineer}}. They are technically excellent. Their reviews have caught real defects that would have corrupted viewing data, and other teams trust the code because they guard it. But {{signal}}. Their comments are usually correct and often curt, and approval usually means rewriting the change their way. You are {{role}}.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you gather evidence beyond anecdote, how and when you talk to them, what you change in how review works (ownership, written standards, design discussion before code), how you keep the quality they bring, what you do for the engineers affected, and what you do if nothing changes. Then tell me about a real time you dealt with a colleague whose behaviour slowed others down, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Their expertise is needed; losing them would hurt. The other engineers' growth and retention matter too. What you can do depends on your role.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Gathers evidence (turnaround, rejection reasons, affected people) and separates correctness from preference; holds an early, private, specific conversation about impact and listens for real risks; acts within the authority of their stated role and escalates with evidence only when needed; turns implicit standards into written ones, adds design discussion before code and shares review ownership while keeping the bar on critical paths; supports the affected engineers; follows through with a clear next step if nothing changes; real example with personal actions and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Has anyone told them?
clarifications.a: Not directly. People complain to each other.

clarifications.q: Are their objections usually right?
clarifications.a: Mostly about correctness, yes; often also about style and approach where several answers would be fine.

clarifications.q: Is anything written down about review standards?
clarifications.a: No. The standard lives in their head.

clarifications.q: Are they aware of the impact?
clarifications.a: Unknown. In a recent retrospective they said review quality is the only thing protecting the data.

hints: Get facts first: review turnaround, rejection reasons, who is affected. Separate correctness objections from preference.
Talk to them privately, early and specifically, about impact, and listen; they may see a real risk others do not.
Turn their standard into something written and shared, so quality no longer depends on one reviewer.
followups: What data would you gather, and what would change your view of the situation?
What do you say in the first conversation, and how do you respond if they say the others' code is simply not good enough?
What would you change in the review process, and how do you keep the quality bar on the changes that matter most?
Two months later nothing has changed. What do you do next, given your role?
In your real example, what changed in the colleague's behaviour, and what did you learn about your own approach?

rules.ask: What exactly do you say in the first two minutes, and what do you expect them to say back?
Before any formal step, what have you tried, and what evidence do you have that it did not work?
Does spreading review ownership lower the bar on the changes that matter most? How would you know?
Who writes the standards, and what happens when the senior engineer disagrees with one of them?
What can you do yourself before you involve someone else, and what would you bring to that conversation?

templates.title: An internal fork of an open-source engine, or contributing upstream
templates.subtopic: open-source forks, upstream contribution, migration risk

engine: an open-source stream-processing engine that runs the playback-event pipelines
an open-source table-format library used by every batch job on viewing data
an open-source workflow scheduler that runs every nightly content-analytics job
behind: a major version and its follow-up releases
trigger: a security fix has been released upstream and does not apply cleanly to the fork
the engineer who maintained most of the local patches has left
a feature the team needs exists upstream but conflicts with two of the fork's patches

sections.scenario: Your organisation runs an internal fork of {{engine}}. It carries {{patches}} local patches (performance fixes, integrations with internal services, and a few behaviour changes other teams now rely on) and is {{behind}} behind upstream. Now {{trigger}}. You have been asked to recommend a direction and lead it: keep the fork and catch up, rebase onto upstream and contribute what can be contributed, or move to a managed offering of the same engine.
sections.problem: How do you decide, and how do you lead it? Cover how you inventory and classify the patches, how you estimate the cost and risk of each option, how you work with the upstream project's maintainers, how you prove a new version behaves the same on your production workloads before switching, how you bring along the teams that rely on the fork's behaviour, and how you handle the immediate trigger while the longer plan runs. Then tell me about a real time you made a build, fork or adopt decision about a dependency, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The engine runs production pipelines that cannot have a long outage. Upstream contributions can take months and may be rejected. You have three engineers for two quarters. Assume your employer permits open-source contributions.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Handles the immediate trigger on a short, separate path; inventories and classifies patches, finding which are already upstream, contributable, replaceable by extension points or truly local; estimates the ongoing cost of each option in engineer time and risk, not only the migration cost; works with upstream maintainers respectfully and plans for rejection; proves equivalence by shadow runs or replays on production workloads with explicit blocking criteria; finds and brings along teams that rely on behaviour changes; real example with cost and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Are the patches documented?
clarifications.a: Partly: commit messages and a wiki page last updated a year ago.

clarifications.q: Have any patches been offered upstream before?
clarifications.a: Two were; one was merged, one stalled in review.

clarifications.q: Does the managed offering support our integrations?
clarifications.a: Most, through public extension points; you would have to check each patch.

clarifications.q: Who relies on the behaviour changes?
clarifications.a: At least four teams, not all of whom know they rely on them.

hints: Classify every patch: already fixed upstream, could be contributed, could become a plugin or configuration, or must stay local. The last group is the fork's true cost.
Deal with the immediate trigger on its own short path, so the long-term choice is not made under pressure.
Prove equivalence on your workloads: replay or shadow-run production jobs on both versions and compare outputs and performance.
followups: How do you estimate what the fork costs per year today, and what each option would cost?
The maintainers reject your largest patch because it does not fit their design. What now?
How do you shadow-run the new version, and what differences would block the switch?
A team discovers during testing that it depends on a behaviour change nobody documented. How do you handle it?
In your real example, what did the decision cost, and would you make it again?

rules.ask: How do you get a patch accepted by maintainers who owe you nothing, and how long do you plan for it?
How do you test that the rebased engine behaves the same on your production workloads before switching?
Which of your local patches does the managed offering lack, and who depends on them?
Which patches can become plugins against public interfaces and which cannot? What happens to the rest?
Do you patch the fork now or wait for the rebase? Who decides, and on what evidence?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for a global, many-region audience
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, scaling to a global multi-region service

angle: the data model and why it held up
the hardest correctness problem you solved
the most important reliability decision you made
global_feature: daily numbers computed for each country's local day
member data kept in particular regions for some countries
regional failover that neither loses nor double counts events
a launch that has to go live in every country at the same moment

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change to serve a global streaming audience in many time zones from {{regions}} cloud regions, and to support {{global_feature}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes when the system runs in {{regions}} regions for a worldwide audience and must support {{global_feature}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The global multi-region setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; an honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible multi-region analysis that places each kind of state, states consistency and failover behaviour, and handles time zones explicitly; a concrete, incremental path to the global feature; own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a data system?
clarifications.a: It should move, store or compute data that others depend on; a service with a significant data model counts.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

clarifications.q: Was my system ever multi-region?
clarifications.a: It does not need to have been; the second half is reasoning, and you should say which parts are.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the global question, start from what "a day", "an event" and "the source of truth" mean when there are {{regions}} regions and two dozen time zones.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Running in {{regions}} regions, where does each piece of state live, and what happens to it when a region fails?
How would you add {{global_feature}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Why that over the obvious alternative, and what did it cost you?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
A country's day ends while another region is still processing yesterday's late events. When is that country's daily number final?
Two regions accept writes for the same record during a network split. What does your system do when they reconnect?
